title: Without going out the door
hook: without going out the door, know the world (Tao Te Ching 47)

segments.voice: Yesterday, content with enough: chapter forty-six says no disaster is greater than not knowing what's enough. Your line was enough is enough. Where did you pause before reaching for more? Day one thousand one hundred nine.

A suitcase sits by the door, half packed. The plan is a trip far away to finally figure things out: a mountain, a coastline, a city where everything will be different. Some people take that trip and come home changed. Some come home with the same questions in a different suitcase. Chapter forty-seven of the Tao Te Ching has something to say to the half-packed bag, and it begins with a door that never opens.
screen: `A HALF-PACKED SUITCASE.` → `FAR AWAY, TO FIGURE IT OUT.` → `A DOOR THAT NEVER OPENS.`

segments.voice: First, the claim. In James Legge's translation, chapter forty-seven opens: "Without going outside his door, one understands (all that takes place) under the sky." It goes on: without looking out of the window, one sees the way of heaven. Second, the warning that follows. Legge again: "The farther that one goes out (from himself), the less he knows." Notice Legge's little bracket, from himself. He reads the going out as going away from yourself, not only as travel. Third, what the chapter is not saying. It doesn't forbid journeys or say that seeing the world is useless. Its point is about where understanding comes from. The sage, it says, knows without traveling, names things without seeing them, and gets things done without forcing. Knowing, in this chapter, happens close to home: in attention, in stillness, in the life right in front of you. Fourth, the room you're in. It's easy to think the answer is somewhere else: a new city, a new job, a retreat across the world, the next video. Sometimes it is. But chapter forty-seven points at the kitchen, the window, the street you walk every day, the people already in the house. A cup of tea drunk slowly at your own table can teach something a long flight can't. The chapter's suggestion is simple: before going out the door to look for the world, look at the room you're in.
screen: `WITHOUT GOING OUT THE DOOR.` · `THE FARTHER OUT, THE LESS YOU KNOW.` · `NOT A BAN ON JOURNEYS.` · `THE ROOM YOU'RE IN.` · then, large: `AT HOME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: learn from staying home. Stay exactly where you are. Look slowly around the room, or the car, or the bench, as if you'd traveled a long way to see it. The light on one wall. A sound from outside. The texture of whatever you're sitting on. Then close your eyes and turn the same attention inward, to the breath, to the weight of your body. Nothing to go out and get. The bell holds the time.
Without going out the door. Chapter forty-seven: without going outside the door, one understands the world, and the farther one goes out from oneself, the less one knows. Today's word.
screen: `WITHOUT GOING OUT THE DOOR — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: at home. Before you look for an answer somewhere far away today, spend five minutes looking for it right where you live. Day one thousand one hundred nine.

howItsDone: Readers of the Tao Te Ching often take chapter forty-seven as a reason to look for insight in stillness and in ordinary home life, rather than only in travel or new experiences.
